name: Project Drawdown (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: a tonne of greenhouse gas kept out of the air spares people everywhere (heat deaths), so the result is spread by world population.
summary: Project Drawdown (Saint Paul, Minnesota) researches which climate solutions matter most (Drawdown Explorer, the Drawdown Roadmap) and guides philanthropists, companies and investors toward them, with storytelling for the public; this model values that information as the money (and people's choices) it changed in 2023-2025 times the difference in tonnes per dollar between where the money went and where it would have gone, against its spending over those years ($6.0M in 2025). At the defaults a dollar given averts about 0.003 tonnes of CO₂e, 0.0017 years of healthy life per $1,000, nearly all of it from funders' grants it redirected; it is low because a redirected dollar is credited only for its gain over the old use, and much of the shift would have happened anyway or is others' doing. The result is mostly uncertainty: how much giving it changes, how much better the new use is, and the shared years a changed choice counts; every branch is discounted for missing data, since no decision it changed is counted or followed up.

Philanthropy for climate mitigation worldwide, 2024 (foundations and individuals)

source.title: ClimateWorks Foundation, Funding trends 2026: Climate change mitigation philanthropy
source.quote: reached an estimated $11.7 billion to $18.4 billion in 2024
source.note: Best guess the range's middle. Foundations alone gave $6 billion ('Foundation funding for climate mitigation reached $6 billion for the first time in 2024').

rows.explainer: ClimateWorks' estimate of all foundation and individual giving to climate mitigation in 2024, the pool whose allocation Drawdown's research and guidance can change; its own range.

rows.label: Philanthropy: share of that giving newly reallocated each year after funders used Drawdown's work
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 0.3% a year (0.05% to 1.5%): about $45M of new decisions a year, gross, before what would have happened anyway and others' part. Anchors: its own claims that the Drawdown Capital Coalition and its science have 'helped guide billions of dollars' (annual update p. 6; cumulative since 2017, and 'guided' money includes money that already went there); funders who say they built their climate strategy on it (the Mighty Arrow Family Foundation, the Ray C. Anderson Foundation, ReFED on food-waste funding, Toniic's members, annual update p. 15); its reach (115,000 newsletter subscribers, 12,500 downloads of its publications a year, 2 million views of its videos, year-end report p. 9). Its own funders, foundations giving $4M-$7M a year, are among the readers. Only decisions made in 2023-2025 count: earlier ones (funds formed after the 2017 book) are outside the period.

rows.label: Philanthropy: giving newly reallocated each year (gross)
Companies: corporate climate spending newly reallocated each year (gross)
rows.explainer: Our judgment, $15M a year ($2M to $100M), gross: what companies that worked with Drawdown Labs or its job-function guides changed in their climate budgets each year (from offsets and carbon accounting toward cutting their own and their suppliers' emissions, the 'emergency brake' solutions and policy support it recommends). Anchors: its partners and readers include Google, General Mills, Intuit, LinkedIn, Mars (whose staff climate training used its content, year-end report p. 9) and Microsoft's sustainability team (annual update p. 4); Drawdown Labs cost $0.8M in 2025; large companies' climate budgets run to tens or hundreds of millions, but most of it is set by regulation, targets and prices, and no company names an amount Drawdown changed.

rows.label: Investors: climate investment newly reallocated each year (gross)
rows.explainer: Our judgment, $100M a year ($10M to $1B), gross: investment that impact investors, funds and venture firms newly steered using its solutions list in 2023-2025. Anchors: the Carbon Collective US Climate Solutions ETF (almost $40M under management) picks companies earning half their revenue from Drawdown-recommended solutions (year-end report p. 10); Toniic's members use it for climate investments (annual update p. 15); 'numerous' funds and venture firms credit it (year-end report p. 9). Investment is large beside giving, but a tilt in what investors buy changes little (the next rows).

rows.label: Public: people who newly take a lasting climate action each year because of its stories and guides
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 3,000 people a year (300 to 30,000): Drawdown's Neighborhood, the Global Solutions Diary, Climate Solutions 101 and the SHIFT guide to individual action reached 2 million video views and 300,000 social-media followers (year-end report p. 9); about one view in a thousand leading to a lasting change of one household's emissions. No survey of what viewers did.

rows.label: Philanthropy: tonnes of CO₂e a climate grant achieves where it would have gone
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 0.01 tonnes a dollar ($100 a tonne; 0.002 to 0.04): an ordinary climate grant, most of which funds advocacy, research and programmes in the US and Europe. Cross-check, not an input: the site's own models of the large climate advocacy groups count 0.015 to 0.035 tonnes per dollar of their spending (Clean Air Task Force, Environmental Defense Fund, Earthjustice, the Sierra Club Foundation, the Union of Concerned Scientists), before the next-dollar step; deployment grants buy tonnes at abatement costs of roughly $20-$200 a tonne. Tonnes counted the site's way, each grant's own waits already in them.

rows.label: Philanthropy: how much more a reallocated dollar achieves than where it would have gone
rows.explainer: Our judgment, +30% (+3% to +150%): Drawdown points funders to work its research finds big and underfunded (methane, refrigerants and black carbon, the 'emergency brake'; food and farming emissions, which get 3% of climate funding, annual update p. 5; deforestation), and away from 'unproven or untargeted' work. Cost-effectiveness between climate areas differs several-fold, but its rankings were long by total potential, not by what a further dollar does (Drawdown Explorer adds cost per tonne from 2025), funders move within their own missions, and a shift can as well go to a crowded field: so a modest gain, with a range near nothing at the low end.

rows.label: Philanthropy: difference in tonnes per dollar reallocated
rows.explainer: The difference between the options: the better option's tonnes per dollar less the old one's.

rows.label: Companies: tonnes of CO₂e a corporate climate dollar achieves where it would have gone
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 0.01 tonnes a dollar (0.002 to 0.04): what companies' climate budgets buy, renewable-energy certificates that add little new power, offsets of which a review of credits found under a sixth to be real cuts (Probst et al. 2024, Nature Communications), efficiency at $20-$200 a tonne. About the same as a climate grant, the range as wide.

rows.label: Companies: how much more a reallocated corporate dollar achieves
rows.explainer: Our judgment, +30% (+3% to +150%), as for philanthropy: it pushes companies from carbon accounting and offsets to cutting emissions and supporting policy; cheap offsets are not all worthless, and its guides are general (job-function checklists), so the gain is modest.

rows.label: Companies: difference in tonnes per dollar reallocated
Investors: difference in tonnes per dollar of investment reallocated
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 0.0003 tonnes per dollar (0.00003 to 0.003): an invested dollar is lent or bought, not spent, and comes back. Buying listed climate-solution shares instead of others hardly changes companies' cost of capital or emissions (Berk and van Binsbergen 2021, 'The impact of impact investing'); venture and project finance can add capacity that wouldn't be built, at most a few per cent of an equivalent grant's tonnes (0.01 a dollar, above). Most of the money counted is listed funds.

rows.label: Public: tonnes of CO₂e a year one lasting household action cuts
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 0.5 tonnes a year (0.1 to 2): the high-impact individual actions (Wynes and Nicholas 2017, Environmental Research Letters) cut 0.8 (a plant-based diet) to 2.4 (living car-free) tonnes a year each, one transatlantic flight 1.6; most changes are partial (eating less meat, one flight fewer, a heat pump some years early).

rows.label: Probability the change happens because of this work
rows.explainer: 1: the branches count money and people whose choices did change, not a chance of a change; whether they would have changed anyway is the counterfactual below.

rows.label: Years a won reform counts before it would have come anyway
rows.explainer: The site's one answer (docs/normalization.md 2.9): a funder's, company's or person's changed choice counts as long as a won reform, the years it was brought forward by.

rows.label: Years from the decision until the reallocated money is spent
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 1 year (0.5 to 3): a funder's new strategy reaches grants in its next cycle, a company's in its next budget. The tonnes per dollar above already count each option's own waits (the site's climate models discount them), so only this wait is added; discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the tonnes are avoided
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate; the unit's conversion then discounts the heat deaths from the year the tonne is avoided, so nothing is discounted twice.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity), a multiplier
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 0.7 (0.4 to 0.95), as for the site's other research and meta builds (0.7): the money and people counted rest on testimonials Drawdown selected and on no follow-up of what the readers did differently; and its recommendations could point some money to worse options, which the gains above only partly allow for.

rows.label: Philanthropy: share of the reallocation that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 50% (25% to 80%): funders have other guides to the same areas (ClimateWorks, the IPCC, Founders Pledge and Giving Green, the Global Methane Hub, their own staff), and methane and food were rising up funders' agendas anyway; a funder that read Drawdown first might have reached much the same choice within a few years.

rows.label: Companies: share of the reallocation that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 45% (20% to 75%): companies get the same advice from the Science Based Targets initiative, consultants and their own teams, and regulation (Europe's reporting rules) pushes the same way.

rows.label: Investors: share of the reallocation that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 40% (15% to 80%): many lists of climate-solution companies exist (index providers' climate indices, the EU taxonomy); a fund built on Drawdown's list would mostly hold the same companies on another's.

rows.label: Public: share of the changes that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 50% (20% to 80%): the people who watch climate-solution stories are already engaged and get the same ideas from other media.

rows.label: Philanthropy: Drawdown's share of the resources behind the reallocation
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 30% (10% to 60%): the funders' own staff and advisers and the grantees pitching to them work on the same decision; Drawdown supplies the evidence and, through the Capital Coalition, some of the advice.

rows.label: Philanthropy: Drawdown's share of credit used behind the reallocation
rows.explainer: Its share of the resources; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Companies: Drawdown's share of the resources behind the reallocation
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 15% (5% to 40%): a company's own sustainability staff, consultants and the employees who take its guides do most of the work of a change; Drawdown's guides and training are one input.

rows.label: Companies: Drawdown's share of credit used behind the reallocation
rows.explainer: Its share of the resources; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Investors: Drawdown's share of the resources behind the reallocation
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 10% (3% to 30%): the fund managers build, sell and run the funds; Drawdown's free list is one input (Carbon Collective calls it its 'guidepost', year-end report p. 10).

rows.label: Investors: Drawdown's share of credit used behind the reallocation
rows.explainer: Its share of the resources; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Public: Drawdown's share of the resources behind the changes
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 50% (20% to 80%): the people changing pay the cost themselves (counted in the tonnes, not as a resource); other groups' outreach shares the prompting.

rows.label: Public: Drawdown's share of credit used behind the changes
rows.explainer: Its share of the resources; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): no decision Drawdown changed is counted or followed up; the money, the gains and its part in them are judgments. Every branch takes it.

rows.label: Side effect: other good the branches leave out, as a share of the modelled value
rows.explainer: Our judgment, +15% (+3% to +40%): its advice to policymakers (COP meetings, local and national governments, year-end report p. 9) with no named policy won; research others cite (the World Resources Institute, the Global Methane Hub, the UN climate secretariat); companies founded on its work; and its new Drawdown Nexus work on climate, nature and wellbeing together. Below the communications and research share of its spending, since most of that work reaches people through the branches.

rows.label: Side effect: companies using the partnership as cover, as a share of the modelled value
rows.explainer: Our judgment, -3% (-10% to 0): a company working with Drawdown Labs can cite it in its reputation while lobbying against climate rules or cutting little; Drawdown says donors have no role in its research and it endorses no solution for money (year-end report p. 15).

rows.label: Philanthropy: methane's share of the tonnes
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 30% (10% to 50%): its 'emergency brake' advice puts methane first (landfills, farming, oil and gas), with food waste and refrigerants (counted as CO₂e here too).

rows.label: Investors: methane's share of the tonnes
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 5% (1% to 15%): climate-solution companies are mostly clean power, transport and efficiency.

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths per tonne of this fuel, relative to the fossil-fuel average
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 0.14 of the fossil-fuel average behind the shared rate (0.03 to 0.5): most of the money counted is spent in the US and Europe (60% of single-region foundation climate funding, ClimateWorks), whose fuel tonnes carry little smoke (US power 0.013, US coal plants 0.067, US cars 0.04: facts: climate); the rest in Asia, Africa and Latin America, where coal, kerosene and cooking fires carry several times the average. Weighted about two-thirds to one-third.
